Release Number 9325-26
CFTC Files Lawsuit Against Arkansas as the Agency Defends its Federal Jurisdiction Over Prediction Markets 
November 13, 2026
WASHINGTON — The Commodity Futures Trading Commission today announced that it has filed a lawsuit against Arkansas to block the state’s attempts to halt event-contract trading and impose up to hundreds of millions of dollars in civil penalties on CFTC-registered exchanges. 
Arkansas is bringing a civil enforcement against Kalshi in state court, a CFTC-designated contract market. Arkansas’s efforts to obstruct the functions of CFTC-registered exchanges operating lawfully under the Commodity Exchange Act are preempted by federal law. 
“As prediction markets continue to prove their value in being useful for risk management and providing the public with valuable information about the future, Arkansas seeks to shut down event contracts ranging from sports and politics to other important world events,” said Chairman Michael S. Selig. “The CFTC will continue to defend its sole jurisdiction over these federally regulated markets as granted by Congress under the Commodity Exchange Act, and the Commission will not let state interference thwart its regulatory efforts and destroy federally regulated markets.” 
Arkansas is the 11th state the CFTC has sued to vindicate federal sovereign interests. The CFTC has also submitted amicus briefs in four federal Courts of Appeal and one state Supreme Court.

Explanatory Note 
On November 13, 2026, Virgin Galactic Holdings, Inc. (the “Company”) announced a series of transactions described in this Current Report under Items 3.02 and 8.01 as part of its previously disclosed comprehensive plan to support its operations and growth initiatives as it prepares for the expected commencement of its commercial flights in 2027. This plan includes (1) improving working capital, including to fund its operations leading up to and following the start of commercial service, (2) investing in growth initiatives, including (a) the construction of a new high-cadence launch hangar and fueling infrastructure expected to increase the Company’s spaceflight capacity and (b) the expansion of its rocket production capabilities to support higher rate production and to pursue additional market opportunities, and (3) repaying a portion of its outstanding indebtedness. The exchange described under Item 3.02, if completed, will reduce the aggregate principal amount of the Company’s outstanding 2.50% Convertible Senior Notes due 2027 and the amount of cash that the Company would otherwise be required to pay for principal of, and interest on, the exchanged notes, and the indenture amendment described under Item 8.01 provides the Company with greater flexibility in the use of the net cash proceeds from the sale of certain of its assets to support this plan. 
 | Item 3.02.
 | 
Unregistered Sales of Equity Securities. 
On November 13, 2026, the Company entered into a privately negotiated exchange agreement with a holder of its 2.50% Convertible Senior Notes due 2027 (the “2027 Notes”) to exchange (the “Exchange”) approximately $12.5 million in aggregate principal amount of 2027 Notes held by such holder for the Shares (as defined below). 
The holder of the 2027 Notes has agreed to accept the Shares in lieu of the cash payment obligation that it otherwise would be entitled to receive for the principal and interest under the 2027 Notes. Following the completion of the Exchange, the Company will reduce the outstanding 2027 Notes by approximately 69.7%, from $17.9 million to $5.4 million in aggregate principal amount outstanding. The remaining 2027 Notes outstanding following the Exchange represent approximately 1.3% of the $425.0 million in aggregate principal amount of 2027 Notes originally issued in January 2022. 
The Exchange is expected to close on or about November 19, 2026 (the “Closing Date”), subject to the satisfaction of customary closing conditions. On the Closing Date, the Company will issue shares of the Company’s common stock (collectively, the “Shares”), the number of which will be determined over a two-day observation period beginning on November 17, 2026. One half (1/2) of the sum of (i) the aggregate principal amount of the 2027 Notes to be exchanged plus (ii) accrued and unpaid interest thereon to, but excluding, February 1, 2027, will be divided by the daily volume-weighted average price of the common stock (the “Daily VWAP”) for each respective trading day during the observation period. The two daily amounts will then be added together, and the resulting total number of Shares will be issued to the holder on the Closing Date. 
The Daily VWAP will be subject to (i) a floor of no lower than 85% and (ii) a cap of no higher than 115%, in each case, of the closing price of the Company’s common stock on November 16, 2026. The Daily VWAP will solely be used to determine the total number of Shares to be issued to the holder and will not impact the principal amount of the 2027 Notes being exchanged. 
The issuance of the Shares by the Company is being made in reliance on the exemption from the registration requirements of the Securities Act of 1933, as amended (the “Securities Act”), provided by Section 4(a)(2) of the Securities Act. The Shares will be issued only to investors that qualify as “qualified institutional buyers” (as such term is defined in Rule 144A under the Securities Act) and institutional “accredited investors” (as such term is defined in Rule 501 of Regulation D under the Securities Act). The Shares have not been registered under the Securities Act or the securities laws of any state or other jurisdiction, and may not be offered or sold in the United States absent registration or an applicable exemption from the registration requirements of the Securities Act and such other jurisdictions. 
 | Item 8.01.
 | 
Other Events. 
On November 13, 2026, after receiving the requisite consent of holders of its 9.80% First Lien Notes due 2028 (the “First Lien Notes”), the Company amended certain provisions of the indenture governing the First Lien Notes to, among other things, permit the Company to sell certain assets without such sale triggering the indenture’s requirement to use the sale proceeds to redeem the First Lien Notes. The Company paid no consent fee to the holders of the First Lien Notes for such consent. 
In exchange for such consent, the Company agreed to redeem First Lien Notes in a principal amount equal to 80% of the net cash proceeds of any such asset sale above $5 million if such asset sale occurs by July 30, 2027. The redemption price will be 100% of the principal amount redeemed, plus accrued and unpaid interest, and will be payable, at the Company’s election, in cash or shares of its common stock (up to a maximum of 2,230,425 shares). The Company has previously reduced the outstanding balance of its First Lien Notes from $212.5 million at issuance in December 2025 to $172.0 million and satisfied all scheduled principal payments prior to the scheduled amortization payment due on March 31, 2028. Following any such redemption, the Company expects to reduce the amount required for the March 31, 2028 amortization payment. 
There can be no assurance that the Company will sell such assets, or as to the timing or proceeds of any sale.

The Bank of England, the Monetary Authority of Singapore, and the Bank of Thailand: Project Meridian FX APAC 
 Joint media release 
 Published on 
 13 November 2026 
News Release
The Bank of England, the Monetary Authority of Singapore, and the Bank of Thailand today published the findings from their collaboration on foreign exchange (FX) settlement under Project Meridian FX APAC.footnote [1]
The project showed that synchronisation – a service that coordinates movements of central bank money – could be one approach to supporting interoperability across wholesale settlement environments built on different technologies and operating models. This marks significant progress in making cross-border FX transactions safer and more efficient, and supporting interoperability as different forms of money evolve in different ways. In light of the Bank of England’s plans to launch a live synchronisation interface in 2028,footnote [2] the findings provide valuable insight into how the approach could be developed into a live service.
Building on the earlier work,footnote [3] Project Meridian FX APAC tested payment-versus-payment FX settlementfootnote [4] and multilateral net FX across the three central banks’ test environments, spanning both Real-Time Gross Settlement and Distributed Ledger Technology-based settlement systems. The project encompassed a wider range of currencies, technologies, infrastructures and time zones. Partior, the project’s delivery partner, developed, integrated and tested the Synchronisation Operatorfootnote [5] prototype for the trial.
The trial demonstrated that synchronised settlement can be achieved across central bank systems with different technologies and capabilities, while identifying the requirements and trade-offs involved. They also demonstrated how multilateral net FX settlement can support banks in using their liquidity more efficiently by netting payments against each other.
The project also examined the legal, regulatory and oversight considerations for applying synchronised FX settlement across diverse wholesale settlement systems. The analysis was informed by perspectives from the Reserve Bank of Australia and Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, who participated as observer central banks.
The project’s findings and insights are published across three complementary reports: Introduction and Executive Summary, Technical Report, and Policy Report. Together, they set out the experimental results, key technical findings and policy considerations.
These results provide insights for further exploration of synchronisation as a means of enabling safer and more efficient FX settlement across diverse wholesale settlement systems. Future work could involve extending the existing approach to additional jurisdictions and industry participants, a wider range of currencies and transaction scenarios, and further consider the legal arrangements needed in practice.
Tom Mutton, Executive Director of Payments, Innovation and Fintech at the Bank of England, said, ‘Innovation has the greatest impact when it addresses real world challenges. Project Meridian FX APAC provides practical evidence of how synchronised settlement could help reduce risk and improve efficiency in cross-border FX transactions. The results provide a strong foundation for further collaboration as we explore how this approach could be developed towards real-world use’.
Kenneth Gay, Chief FinTech Officer at the Monetary Authority of Singapore, said, ‘Cross-border settlement increasingly takes place across systems built on different technologies and operating models. Project Meridian FX APAC has shown how synchronisation could help enable PvP settlement across these diverse environments, reducing settlement risk while supporting greater interoperability’.
Pucktada Treeratpituk, Director of Payment Systems and Financial Technology Policy Department at the Bank of Thailand, said, ‘Project Meridian FX APAC successfully demonstrated that synchronisation can work across diverse wholesale settlement systems, making cross-border FX safer and more efficient while preserving trust in central bank money. The insights on technical integration, operating models and regulatory considerations established a practical foundation for modernising wholesale settlement infrastructure’.
About the Bank of England
The Bank of England, established in 1694, is the central bank of the United Kingdom. It is responsible for maintaining monetary and financial stability. In this capacity, the Bank of England undertakes a range of functions, including the implementation of monetary policy, oversight of payment systems, prudential regulation of financial institutions, and the issuance of currency. The Bank of England also plays a key role in safeguarding financial stability through its work on systemic risk, resolution frameworks, and market operations. In relation to UK payments, the Bank of England performs a number of operational functions, including acting as the operator of the UK’s Real-Time Gross Settlement (RTGS) system and the CHAPS payment system.
About the Monetary Authority of Singapore
The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) is Singapore’s central bank and integrated financial regulator. As a central bank, MAS promotes sustained, non-inflationary economic growth through the conduct of monetary policy and close macroeconomic surveillance and analysis. It manages Singapore’s exchange rate, official foreign reserves, and liquidity in the banking sector. As an integrated financial supervisor, MAS fosters a sound financial services sector through its prudential oversight of all financial institutions in Singapore – banks, insurers, capital market intermediaries, financial advisors and financial market infrastructure. It is also responsible for well-functioning financial markets, sound conduct, and investor education. MAS also works with the financial industry to foster the growth of Singapore as an international financial centre.
About the Bank of Thailand
The Bank of Thailand (BOT) is the central bank and regulator of financial services in Thailand. The BOT is responsible for maintaining monetary stability, financial institution system stability and payment systems stability. In relation to Thailand payments, the BOT functions as the operator of the Bank of Thailand Automated High-value Transfer Network (BAHTNET), which constitutes a core financial infrastructure facilitating high-value funds transfer on a RTGS basis.

 This project, to explore the technical and policy implications of settling foreign exchange (FX) transactions using synchronised settlement mechanisms, was announced in November 2025. 
 The Bank of England announced their intention to launch a live synchronisation interface in 2028, as part of their Call for Input on the Future of Tokenisation with the FCA. For further information on the Bank of England’s synchronisation plans, see Synchronisation | Bank of England – the UK's central bank. 
 Project Meridian FX, led by the BIS Innovation Hub London in collaboration with the Bank of England, Bank of France, Deutsche Bundesbank, Bank of Italy and European Central Bank, tested synchronisation as a solution to cross-border interoperability. Refer to Project Meridian FX: exploring synchronised settlement in FX for more information. 
 PvP settlement reduces FX settlement risk by ensuring that the transfer of one currency occurs if and only if the transfer of the other currency also occurs. SPEECH
Made in Europe
Speech by Isabel Schnabel, Member of the Executive Board of the ECB, at the Economics Conference, Bank of Lithuania
Vilnius, 13 November 2026
We are living through a period of radical transformation. Technological progress is accelerating alongside profound geopolitical shifts, rewriting the rules that have governed global growth, trade and security for decades.[1]
In this polarised world, Europe is often portrayed as a continent in decline, squeezed between geopolitical rivals, held back by excessive regulation and struggling to keep pace with rapid technological change. 
In my remarks this morning, I will argue that although this narrative is appealing in its simplicity, it is misleading.
By many measures, Europe is among the regions with the highest quality of life, grounded in strong institutions, a high degree of social protection and an exceptional capacity to adapt in times of crisis.
Europe can build on these fundamentals to become even stronger. 
I will explain that the key is to unlock the full potential of the Single Market – one of Europe’s most powerful assets – to deliver what Europe lacks today: not talent, not ideas, not research – but scale. 
A 28th regime would be a true game changer in this respect. 
By giving firms seamless access to the entire European market, it would provide the scale needed to convert innovation into economic growth. It would allow Europe to compete as one economy rather than 27, and help create something Europe has long been missing: a true “Made in Europe” brand. 
Europe leading the way in quality of life and democratic values
Europe stands out globally for its quality of life, built on strong economic, social and institutional foundations.
Happiness and life satisfaction in Europe consistently rank among the highest in the world (Slide 2). This goes beyond income or wealth – it reflects the broader conditions that allow people to live secure, fulfilling and prosperous lives.
Social protection, accessible public infrastructure, high-quality public education and family support help turn economic prosperity into tangible improvements in people’s lives.[2]
Health outcomes are particularly revealing here. 
A child born in Spain or Italy can expect to live five years longer than a child born in the United States (Slide 3), despite the United States spending a far larger share of GDP on healthcare than any other advanced economy. Even among the wealthiest Americans, mortality rates are merely at the level of the poorest populations in parts of Europe.[3]
Europeans also benefit from strong institutions. A growing share of the world’s population now lives under de facto autocratic rule, while attacks on democratic freedoms continue at an alarming pace (Slide 4). 
Against this backdrop, Europe’s continued commitment to democracy, the rule of law and institutional checks and balances underpin trust and policy credibility, while independent media ensure accountability and transparency. 
These institutions and principles give people confidence in their future and in the fairness of society, even in the face of adversity. 
Rethinking the transatlantic prosperity gap: more leisure time, greater equality
So, throughout its history, Europe has made deliberate choices about the kind of society it wants to be. But while these choices have resulted in better life outcomes, they have also weighed on GDP per capita, adjusted for the cost of living, which is one of the most used indicators of economic prosperity. 
By this measure, the euro area ranks below other advanced economies (Slide 5).[4]
Part of this difference reflects the fact that some euro area economies are still catching up, mainly in eastern Europe. These countries are mostly growing rapidly, but their incomes remain below the euro area average, which dampens the headline number.
Yet, a substantial gap remains even for the more advanced euro area economies. Interpreting this gap requires careful analysis along three dimensions.[5]
First, a large part of the gap in income levels reflects less work rather than less productive work.
On average, an employee in the United States works around 40 days more per year than an employee in the euro area (Slide 6, left-hand side).[6]
A simple counterfactual shows that if Europeans were to work as many hours as Americans, holding productivity per hour and the employment rate constant, euro area real GDP per capita would be 21% higher.[7] That would close about two-thirds of the current real income gap with the United States (Slide 6, right-hand side).[8] 
So, part of the observed difference in relative income levels reflects preferences and institutions rather than low productivity. Shorter working weeks, more generous vacation entitlements and a higher prevalence of part-time employment in Europe are the result of institutional, social and personal choices. 
Second, growth in Europe is more inclusive. 
Real GDP per capita is an average across regions, individuals and sectors, which means that very high incomes at the top of the distribution can pull the mean upwards.
In the United States, the top 10% of earners today account for around 37% of national income after taxes, a considerable rise since 1980 (Slide 7, left-hand side).[9] In the euro area the share is significantly lower, around 27% on average. 
So, in the United States, a large share of income does not accrue to 90% of the population. The typical American lives in a USD 45,000 economy, not a USD 67,000 one.[10]
This difference also reflects that recent income gains are increasingly concentrated in certain sectors and regions.
Since 2000, more than a quarter of total growth in value added per employee in the United States has accrued in the information and communications technology sector – an industry that accounts for less than 2% of total employment (Slide 7, right-hand side). 
As the exceptional expansion of large technology companies has been concentrated in a small number of US states, the growth performance of the typical state has been more modest, even as aggregate US GDP per capita has surged.
Indeed, growth in real GDP per capita in the median US state and that in the median euro area country have evolved largely in lockstep (Slide 8). 
Standard GDP per capita comparisons thus overstate the disparity in living standards between the United States and the euro area. Europeans work fewer hours, enjoy stronger social protection and live in more equal societies.
But to protect these advantages, Europe needs sustained growth. And this growth is threatened by persistently weak productivity growth in the euro area – the third dimension. 
Over the past three decades, output per hour worked has risen more slowly than in several peer economies, reflecting less capital deepening, smaller firms and the lack of diffusion of new technologies (Slide 9).[11]
This divergence in productivity growth has led to a gradual widening of GDP per capita gaps over time. As productivity growth is the key driver of sustainable improvements in living standards, closing this gap has rightly become a key policy priority in Europe.[12]
The thriving South: from crisis economies to growth leaders
The benefits of addressing structural headwinds are clearly visible in parts of the currency union. 
Take the south of the euro area. 
A decade ago, this region was synonymous with crises, austerity and soaring unemployment. Today, those countries are among the fastest-growing economies in Europe (Slide 10, left-hand side). 
They have been attracting record levels of investment (Slide 10, right-hand side), unemployment has been declining at an impressive pace (Slide 11, left-hand side) and financing conditions relative to Germany, despite some recent spread widening, remain close to their most favourable levels since the global financial crisis of 2008, reflecting economic convergence and financial integration (Slide 11, right-hand side).
As a result, these economies have been able to create space to reduce deficits without undermining the recovery, thereby supporting fiscal consolidation and improving debt sustainability (Slide 12, left-hand side).
To a large extent, the momentum in the southern periphery reflects a sustained improvement in underlying economic capacity. According to the European Commission, potential growth in Spain, Portugal and Greece is projected to be measurably higher than the euro area average in the years to come (Slide 12, right-hand side).
Spain, for example, has emerged as a European leader in renewable energy. This has significantly reduced wholesale electricity prices and the country’s vulnerability to global energy price shocks, transforming it into a European hub for the energy-intensive industries of the future.[13]
Ireland, meanwhile, has become a global hotspot for technology, pharmaceutical and life science companies. It is one of the most efficient countries in which to do business and it has the highest share of tertiary students in natural sciences, mathematics and statistics fields in the EU.
This transformation is the outcome of political choices and social resilience. These economies had to endure painful adjustments when structural change was unfolding, and the population was willing to embrace these changes.
This is partly also a European success story. 
Through instruments such as Next Generation EU, substantial common resources were mobilised to support investment, accelerate reforms and strengthen growth potential in countries that had limited fiscal space to overcome the COVID-19 pandemic.
Stagnating Germany: export-driven business model no longer viable in a fragmenting world 
So, the narrative that Europe is underperforming does not hold up in large parts of the currency union.
Today, economic headwinds are felt most acutely in the euro area’s traditional core, albeit for different reasons. 
In France, efforts to reduce the fiscal deficit have stalled due to political resistance. Sustained consolidation will depend on striking a careful balance between reduced spending and growth-enhancing policies, a task which will require difficult political compromises.
Some northern European countries have struggled to regain momentum after the pandemic. Austria, for example, was in recession both in 2023 and 2024 and grew only moderately in 2025.
Most attention has, however, focused on Germany, which has been navigating an extended period of subdued growth. From 2019 to 2024, its real GDP per capita fell by 0.5%.
The headwinds are numerous. Demographic change is increasingly weighing on potential growth and thus on the sustainability of social security systems (Slide 13, left-hand side). Energy costs remain elevated compared with pre-pandemic levels. And protectionism as well as global competition, especially from China, are hitting Germany particularly hard (Slide 13, right-hand side).
As export growth has softened, Germany’s economic weakness is often attributed to a deterioration in competitiveness. While this has played a role, treating eroding export market shares as the main cause of stagnation is a misdiagnosis of the problem. 
In fact, Germany’s export performance neither dramatically outpaced its peers before the pandemic, nor has it materially lagged behind since (Slide 14, left-hand side).[14] Over the past ten years, Germany’s real goods exports have broadly tracked the global cycle.

On November 12, 2026, the Company closed its public offering of the notes.
The notes were issued under an indenture, dated as of August 19, 2010 (the “Base Indenture”), between the Company and U.S. Bank Trust Company, National Association, as trustee (the “Trustee”), as successor to Computershare Trust Company, National Association, as successor to Wells Fargo Bank, National Association, as original trustee, as supplemented by the Twentieth Supplemental Indenture, dated as of November 12, 2026 (the “Twentieth Supplemental Indenture” and, together with the Base Indenture, the “Indenture”), among the Company, the Trustee, as trustee, registrar and transfer agent, and U.S. Bank Europe DAC, UK Branch, as paying agent (the “Paying Agent”). In connection with the issuance of the notes, the Company also entered into a paying agency agreement (the “Paying Agency Agreement”), dated as of November 12, 2026, among the Company, the Paying Agent and the Trustee, as trustee, registrar and transfer agent. The Twentieth Supplemental Indenture includes the form of the notes. The net proceeds of the offering of the notes are expected to be used for general corporate purposes, which may include working capital, capital expenditures, acquisitions, repayment of indebtedness, including the repayment at or prior to maturity of the Company’s 1.75% Senior Notes due 2027, and other business opportunities.
The notes bear interest at the fixed rate of 4.125% per year and mature on November 12, 2033. Interest on the notes will be due annually on November 12 of each year, commencing November 12, 2027. Prior to August 12, 2033 (three months prior to their maturity date) (the “Par Call Date”), the Company may redeem the notes at its option, in whole or in part, at any time and from time to time, at a redemption price equal to the greater of (i) the make-whole redemption price set forth in the notes less interest accrued to the date of redemption and (ii) 100% of the principal amount of the notes to be redeemed, plus, in either case, accrued and unpaid interest thereon to, but excluding, the redemption date. On or after the Par Call Date, the Company may redeem the notes, in whole or in part, at any time and from time to time, at a redemption price equal to 100% of the principal amount of the notes being redeemed plus accrued and unpaid interest thereon to, but excluding, the redemption date.
Additionally, at the option of the holders of the notes, the Company may be required to purchase all or a portion of the notes upon the occurrence of a “Change of Control Triggering Event” (as defined in the Indenture), at a price equal to 101% of the principal amount thereof, plus accrued and unpaid interest to the date of purchase. 
The Indenture contains covenants that limit the ability of the Company and certain of its subsidiaries to, among other things, incur or create liens and enter into sale and leaseback transactions. In addition, the Indenture contains a covenant that limits the ability of the Company to consolidate or merge with another entity or to sell all or substantially all of its assets to another entity. 
The Indenture contains customary default provisions. In addition, an event of default will occur if the Company or certain of its subsidiaries fail to pay the principal of any Indebtedness (as defined in the Indenture) when due at maturity in an aggregate amount of $50 million or more, or a default occurs that results in the acceleration of the maturity of the Company’s or certain of its subsidiaries’ Indebtedness in an aggregate amount of $50 million or more. Upon the occurrence and during the continuation of an event of default under the Indenture, the notes may become immediately due and payable either automatically or by the vote of the holders of more than 25% of the aggregate principal amount of all of the notes of the applicable series then outstanding.

On November 11, 2026, the Board of Directors of Target Corporation (“Target”) elected Sally Grimes as a director of Target, effective as of December 1, 2026. Ms. Grimes was also appointed to serve on the Audit & Risk Committee and the Infrastructure & Finance Committee, each also effective as of December 1, 2026. 
Ms. Grimes, 55, formerly served as Chief Executive Officer, North America, at Diageo plc, a position she held from September 2023 to March 2026. From May 2020 to February 2023, she was Chief Executive Officer of Clif Bar & Company. Prior to that, Ms. Grimes held other senior leadership positions at Tyson Foods, Inc., including as Group President, Prepared Foods; President, Retail; and Chief Global Growth Officer. Ms. Grimes previously served on the board of directors of Beyond Meat, Inc. from May 2021 to May 2024.
There are no arrangements or understandings between Ms. Grimes and any other person pursuant to which Ms. Grimes was selected as a director of Target. There are no related person transactions within the meaning of Item 404(a) of Regulation S-K promulgated by the Securities and Exchange Commission between Ms. Grimes and Target.

Target Appoints Sally Grimes to Board of Directors
•Grimes is former CEO of Diageo North America, Clif Bar & Company, and Group President at Tyson Foods, bringing extensive experience across consumer brands, innovation, brand building and business transformation.
•Her expertise leading major businesses and partnering with retailers brings additional perspective as Target leads with merchandising authority and elevates its guest experience.
•In joining the board, Grimes will serve on the Audit & Risk and Infrastructure & Finance committees. 
•This appointment is another step in accelerating CEO Michael Fiddelke’s strategy to build the retailer’s next chapter of growth.
MINNEAPOLIS (Nov. 12, 2026) – Target Corporation (NYSE: TGT) today announced that its Board of Directors has elected Sally Grimes as a new independent director, adding experience leading consumer brands, driving innovation and partnering with retailers to create long-term growth.
Grimes is an accomplished executive, having led established and emerging brands through periods of change and growth, with significant experience in innovation and business transformation. She most recently served as CEO North America for Diageo, following her roles as CEO of Clif Bar & Company and Group President at Tyson Foods. Throughout her career, she also built valuable perspective in partnering with retailers to meet consumer needs and business goals. Upon joining Target’s Board, she will serve on the Audit & Risk and Infrastructure & Finance committees.
“Sally has built her career at the intersection of consumer insight, innovation and growth, helping some of the world's most recognized brands anticipate changing needs and bring new ideas to market,” said Michael Fiddelke, Target CEO. “As we sharpen our merchandising authority and continue advancing our strategy, her experience turning consumer trends into compelling products and brands will bring valuable perspective to our Board.”
“An effective Board benefits from leaders who bring different experiences and ways of thinking,” said Christine Leahy, Target’s lead independent director. “Sally combines deep consumer understanding with a track record of innovation, enterprise leadership and business acceleration. That combination complements the strengths already around our board table and 
will be a valuable addition as we provide oversight and counsel on Target’s long-term strategy and growth.”
Grimes also brings public and private company board experience, including service on the boards of Continental Grain Company and Beyond Meat. She currently serves as Executive Director of Knowing NOAH, The Noah John Grimes Family Foundation.
About Target
Target Corporation (NYSE: TGT) brings together style, design and value to offer a distinct assortment and elevated shopping experience across more than 2,000 U.S. stores and online. Powered by more than 400,000 team members, Target serves millions of families each week and invests in the communities where they live and work to support growth and opportunity for all.

On November 12, 2026, Meta Platforms, Inc. (the “Company”) completed an offering of €1,750,000,000 aggregate principal amount of its 4.300% Senior Notes due 2031 (the “2031 Notes”), €1,250,000,000 aggregate principal amount of its 4.650% Senior Notes due 2033 (the “2033 Notes”), €1,000,000,000 aggregate principal amount of its 4.900% Senior Notes due 2035 (the “2035 Notes”), €1,750,000,000 aggregate principal amount of its 5.400% Senior Notes due 2038 (the “2038 Notes”), €1,750,000,000 aggregate principal amount of its 6.050% Senior Notes due 2044 (the “2044 Notes”), and €1,500,000,000 aggregate principal amount of its 6.400% Senior Notes due 2065 (the “2065 Notes” and, together with the 2031 Notes, the 2033 Notes, the 2035 Notes, the 2038 Notes, and the 2044 Notes, the “EUR Notes”). The offering of the EUR Notes was made pursuant to the Company’s Registration Statement on Form S-3 (File No. 333-295425), which Registration Statement relates to the offer and sale on a delayed basis from time to time of an indeterminate amount of the Company’s debt securities. Further information concerning the EUR Notes and related matters is set forth in the Company’s Prospectus Supplement dated November 4, 2026, which was filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission on November 6, 2026. 
In connection with the issuance of the EUR Notes, the Company entered into an Underwriting Agreement dated as of November 4, 2026 (the “Underwriting Agreement”) with Citigroup Global Markets Limited and Morgan Stanley & Co. International plc, as representatives of the several underwriters listed in Schedule II to the Underwriting Agreement. The foregoing description of the Underwriting Agreement is qualified in its entirety by the terms of such agreement, a copy of which is attached hereto as Exhibit 1.1 and is incorporated by reference herein. 
The EUR Notes were issued pursuant to an Indenture with U.S. Bank Trust Company, National Association, as trustee, dated as of August 9, 2022 (the “Base Indenture”), as supplemented by the seventh supplemental indenture thereto, dated as of November 12, 2026 (the “Seventh Supplemental Indenture” and, together with the Base Indenture, the “Indenture”). The Seventh Supplemental Indenture is attached hereto as Exhibit 4.1 and is incorporated by reference herein. The Base Indenture was previously incorporated by reference into the Registration Statement pursuant to Exhibit 4.1 to the Company’s Current Report on Form 8-K filed on August 9, 2022. The forms of the 2031 Notes, the 2033 Notes, the 2035 Notes, the 2038 Notes, the 2044 Notes, and the 2065 Notes are attached hereto as Exhibits 4.2, 4.3, 4.4, 4.5, 4.6, and 4.7, respectively, and are incorporated by reference herein.

On November 10, 2026, Emerson Electric Co. (the “Company”) entered into a pricing agreement (the “Pricing Agreement”) dated November 10, 2026 (incorporating the

The Notes are being sold to the Underwriters at an issue price of 99.264% of the principal amount thereof, and the Underwriters offered the Notes to the public at a price of 99.639% of the
 principal amount thereof. The closing of the transaction is subject to customary closing conditions and is expected to occur on November 13, 2026. The Company is in the process of applying to list the Notes on the New York Stock Exchange.
The Notes are expected to be issued on November 13, 2026, pursuant to an indenture dated as of December 10, 1998 (the “Base Indenture”), between the Company and

 trustee (the “Trustee”), as supplemented by a Fourth Supplemental Indenture to be dated as of November 13, 2026 (the “Fourth Supplemental Indenture”) between the Company and the Trustee. Pursuant to an Agency Agreement to be dated as of November
 13, 2026 (the “Agency Agreement”) relating to the Notes, the Company will appoint U.S. Bank Europe DAC, UK Branch to act as paying agent for the Notes and U.S. Bank Trust Company, National Association to act as registrar and transfer agent for the
 Notes.
The Notes are being offered and sold pursuant to the Company’s automatic shelf registration statement (the “Registration Statement”) on Form S-3 (File No. 333-299935),
 filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission (the “SEC”) on November 9, 2026. The Company has filed with the SEC a prospectus supplement, dated November 10, 2026, together with the accompanying prospectus, dated November 9, 2026, related to
 the offering and sale of the Notes. This Current Report on Form 8‑K adds exhibits to that Registration Statement. This Current Report is not an offer to sell, nor a solicitation of an offer to buy securities, nor shall there be any sale of these
 securities in any state or jurisdiction in which the offer, solicitation or sale would be unlawful prior to the registration or qualification under the securities laws of such state or jurisdiction.
The Company expects the net proceeds from the sale of the Notes to be approximately €744.5 million (or approximately $830.4 million based upon a euro/U.S. dollar exchange
 rate as of November 6, 2026 of €1.00 = $1.1154, as published by the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System)), before deducting estimated expenses of the offering. The Company expects to use the net proceeds primarily to repay the
 Company’s commercial paper borrowings, and also for general corporate purposes. The notes will be senior unsecured obligations and will rank equally with all of the Company’s existing and future unsecured and unsubordinated debt.
The Notes will bear interest at the rate of 4.000% per year. Interest on the Notes is payable on November 13 of each year, beginning on November 13, 2027. The Notes will
 mature on November 13, 2032. Prior to maturity, the Company may redeem any or all of the Notes at any time at the redemption prices described in the Notes. The notes will be issued in minimum denominations of €100,000 and integral multiples of
 €1,000 in excess thereof.

Federal Reserve Board announces pricing, effective January 1, 2027, for payment services the Federal Reserve Banks provide to banks and credit unions, and changes to streamline and adjust their check services 
For release at 1:30 p.m. EST 
 Share 
The Federal Reserve Board on Thursday announced pricing, effective January 1, 2027, for payment services the Federal Reserve Banks provide to banks and credit unions, such as the clearing of checks, automated clearing house (ACH) transactions, instant payments, and wholesale payment and settlement services. 
By law, the Federal Reserve must establish fees to recover the costs, including imputed costs, of providing payment services over the long run. The Federal Reserve expects to recover 101.5 percent of actual and imputed expenses in 2027, including the return on equity that would have been earned if a private-sector firm provided the services. Overall, price changes for 2027 will result in an estimated 1.4 percent average price increase for established, mature services. 
In addition, the Federal Reserve Banks announced changes to streamline and adjust their check services. As described in the request for information on check services issued last year, the volume of checks processed by the Federal Reserve Banks is declining, but checks remain an important payment instrument for many consumers and businesses. The changes were informed by public feedback and ensure that the Federal Reserve Banks continue to provide check services efficiently. The adjustments include optimizing check processing windows during low-volume periods, increasing fees that banks and credit unions pay to process checks, and other operational updates. These changes do not impact consumers' and businesses' ability to pay with or receive checks and only impact how banks and credit unions process checks with Federal Reserve Banks. 
The entire 2027 fee schedule for all of the Federal Reserve's payment services is published on FRBservices.org®. Additional information on the Federal Reserve's payments services, including service usage statistics, is available on the Board's website.

American Inequality and the Future of AI 
 Governor Michael S. Barr 
At Yale University, New Haven, Connecticut 
 Share

Thank you for the opportunity to speak to you today.1 In a speech earlier this year, I explored scenarios in which artificial intelligence (AI) could affect economic inequality, for better or for worse.2 My focus in those remarks was on the AI side of this relationship, and today I would like to return to this topic by first providing some important context about inequality in the United States. 
Inequality is an aspect of every economy, and understanding the extent and evolution of inequality in the United States can help in forming a clear view of the economic outlook and how the economy is likely to react to new developments. Widening inequality may also, depending on many factors, reflect a decline in economic opportunity for many people, which can limit the economy's productive capacity. 
Today, I will begin by summarizing the current state of economic inequality in the United States, assisted by new results from a long-running survey of households conducted by the Federal Reserve, and then show where this fits into the history of inequality over the past century or so. I will explore some of the forces that have shaped inequality, and what these forces may indicate about how AI is likely to affect the way wealth and income are distributed. 
Wealth and Income Inequality Today
Up-to-date and detailed information about inequality in the United States comes from the latest edition of the Federal Reserve's triennial Survey of Consumer Finances, conducted in 2025 and published just last month.3 The survey confirms that both wealth and income are highly concentrated and that inequality is greater for wealth. The top 10 percent by income of households receive almost one-half of all income in the United States and the top 1 percent receive about one-fifth of income.4 As for wealth, the wealthiest 10 percent of households hold nearly three-fourths of all wealth, and the top 1 percent hold about one-third. By contrast, the entire lower half of households, as measured by wealth holdings, have only 2 percent of wealth. Low wealth means it's also harder to get by every day. Another Fed survey of household finances conducted each year, the Survey of Household Economics and Decisionmaking, finds that 31 percent of respondents in 2025 didn't have the cash to cover an emergency expense of $500 or more.5 
Wealth is even more highly concentrated among the very wealthiest. One-third of wealth is held by the upper 1 percent—that's nearly $60 trillion. There is even more concentration at the very top. The households in the upper 0.1 percent, which is only 135,000 individuals and families, own one-sixth of our nation's wealth. A household at the lower edge of the top 1 percent has 75 times as much wealth as the median household in the middle of the distribution—$16.3 million compared with $215,000 for a household in the middle. A household at the lower edge of the 0.1 percent of the wealthiest has 300 times as much wealth as the median household. 
Wealth concentration has increased at the very top. Using Forbes magazine's tally of the 400 wealthiest individuals, together with data from the Survey of Consumer Finances, a rough estimate is that their share of total wealth rose from 3 percent in 2022 to 4 percent in the most recent survey. Forbes counts nearly 1,000 U.S. billionaires.6 
Digging into the sources of widening inequality, the wealth of those at the top is primarily held in the form of business assets. Research using data from the Survey of Consumer Finances back to the 1940s shows that returns on business equity have been a major source of widening wealth inequality over the decades.7 Most of the income for these wealthy households is in capital income—interest, dividends, capital gains, and business profits—rather than wages and salaries. Unlike these higher-income or wealthier households, most income for middle-class households comes from their paychecks. And it's harder to build wealth that way. 
Although the largest asset class for wealthy households is typically stocks and other financial assets, a substantial amount of their capital income also comes from ownership of private businesses. These private businesses come in two broad types: an actively managed business—such as a plumbing business, retail store, or manufacturing firm—and a passive investment in a business, commonly known as private equity. Owning and running a business has long been a way that households become wealthy. But private equity investments are passively run and are typically only open to the wealthiest individuals and families. These private investments have delivered returns to their owners higher than the typical mix of assets held by middle-income households. Private equity investments are 12 percent of the assets of the wealthiest 0.1 percent of households in the most recent Fed survey. 
For households above the median but below the 90th percentile, the most prevalent assets are housing and stocks, but the value of housing equity has grown more slowly than that of business equity. About three-fourths of households in this group have stock holdings, mostly through retirement accounts. Although ownership of publicly traded companies has become more widespread across the income spectrum as 401(k) plans have become common over the past few decades, stock ownership by value remains highly concentrated among the wealthiest households. The group of households in the 50th through the 90th percentiles of wealth hold only 17 percent of all public stocks by value, underscoring how much wealth is concentrated.8 
Finally, on net, households in the bottom half of the wealth distribution hold just over 2 percent of all wealth, an average of $52,000. About 40 percent of them have equity in homes, and nearly 40 percent own business equity, either through a retirement account or as their own business. But the values are low compared with the upper half of households. 
The Evolution of Inequality
By many estimates, today's inequality levels are among the highest in the past 100 years.9 But wealth and income inequality in America have changed significantly over our history, widening and, at times, also narrowing, driven by a variety of factors, including booms and busts in financial assets, structural changes in the economy, and changes in tax and regulatory policy. In the Gilded Age, roughly 1870 to 1910, incomes rose strongly for most people, but it was also the era when large fortunes were accumulated by industrialists and their families. With no income tax or estate tax for the wealthiest and limited public education for everyone, the gap between those at the top and most others widened.10 But over the subsequent decades, especially during the New Deal, legal and institutional change strengthened worker power, and the introduction and broadening of progressive income and estate taxes helped limit the concentration of income and wealth. 
Inequality narrowed in the decades after World War II, an era of fast economic expansion that benefited many households. There were improvements in public education, including the GI Bill, income tax changes that made rates more progressive, and growing unionization that raised wages for workers.11 
Beginning in the late 1970s, however, wealth and income inequality began to increase again. This was a period of slower economic growth and sometimes high inflation. Top income tax rates declined, and fewer households were required to pay the estate tax. As in the 1910s and 1920s, business equity grew as a share of total assets, helping the wealthiest households become wealthier.12 The wealth generated from the typical middle-class asset—housing—increased but at a slower pace than business assets, exacerbated by the decline in housing wealth during the Global Financial Crisis. Over the same period, real wages grew slowly. Moreover, minimum wage laws failed to keep up with inflation and the growth of the economy.13 
The lesson from this history is that the level of inequality in American society is not immutable—it changes over time. These historical patterns suggest that policy choices play a crucial role in shaping inequality levels. Economic growth, technological change, education, and globalization also play key roles.14 
The Evolution of the Labor and Capital Shares of National Income
Some of these trends are most clearly seen in the decline in the share of national income going to labor over the past 25 years. Though individuals and families across the spectrum hold business equity from which they receive income, the main source of income for most households is wages and salaries—labor earnings. Since lower- and middle-income households depend heavily on wages, another useful way of exploring income and wealth inequality is to consider how the share of national income earned from labor has changed over time, compared with income earned from capital—dividends, interest, and private business earnings. 
After World War II, the labor share of national income was fairly steady between 60 percent and 65 percent, but it began falling in fits and starts beginning in 2001. The decline accelerated after the pandemic and has been especially steep in the past year, reaching a record low of 52.8 percent in the second quarter of 2026.15 Some of this reflects measurement issues associated with how income has been allocated to labor and capital over time.16 But, even after adjusting for those factors, there is a clear downward trend. 
Economic research suggests three causes of the decades-long trend in labor versus capital income, each highly relevant to the potential effects of AI on inequality. The first is technological innovations that have reduced demand for labor and decreased wages; the second is the concentration of market power in many industries with a small number of firms; and the third related cause is the reduction in the bargaining power of workers. 
Technology replacing labor has been going on for centuries, but new technology can also augment the productivity of existing jobs and create new jobs, including those that are hard to envision when the technology is initially adopted, a point I have noted in a number of speeches.17 The internet and the businesses it created reduced employment in some occupations—such as travel agents—and eliminated others: Think video store workers. But the development of new technologies has expanded jobs in other areas. Item 5.02 Departure of Directors or Certain Officers; Election of Directors; Appointment of Certain Officers; Compensatory Arrangements of Certain Officers.
On November 11, 2026 the Board of Directors (the "Board") of Marvell Technology, Inc. (the "Company") approved an increase in the size of the Board from seven (7) to ten (10) members and the appointments of Donna C. Morris, Douglas R. Bettinger and Sasan K. Goodarzi to the Board, in each case effective November 12, 2026. Ms. Morris and Mr. Goodarzi have been appointed to the Executive Compensation Committee of the Board, and Mr. Bettinger has been appointed to the Audit Committee of the Board. Each of Ms. Morris, Mr. Bettinger and Mr. Goodarzi will stand for election at the Company's 2027 annual meeting of stockholders.
The Board has determined that each of Ms. Morris, Mr. Bettinger and Mr. Goodarzi is an "independent director" as defined under the applicable rules and regulations of the Securities and Exchange Commission and the listing requirements and rules of The NASDAQ Stock Market. The Board has also determined that Mr. Bettinger satisfies the additional audit committee independence requirements of Rule 10A-3 and Nasdaq Listing Rule 5605(c)(2)(A) and qualifies as an "audit committee financial expert" as defined in Item 407(d)(5) of Regulation S-K. The Board has also determined that each of Ms. Morris and Mr. Goodarzi satisfies the additional independence requirements applicable to members of the Executive Compensation Committee under Nasdaq Listing Rule 5605(d)(2)(A) and Rule 10C-1 under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, as amended, and qualifies as a “non-employee director” within the meaning of Rule 16b-3 thereunder.
Donna C. Morris, age 59, is the Executive Vice President and Chief People Officer of Walmart Inc., a technology-powered omnichannel retailer, a position she has held since February 2020, where she is a member of Walmart's executive committee and leads the company's global people strategy. From April 2002 to January 2020, Ms. Morris held various roles at Adobe Inc., including most recently Chief Human Resources Officer and Executive Vice President, Employee Experience. Ms. Morris previously served as a director of Marvell Technology Group Ltd., the Company's predecessor, from May 2018 until July 2020. She currently serves on the boards of directors of UKG Inc., PhonePe and the Crystal Bridges Museum of American Art, and is a trustee of Fordham University. Ms. Morris holds a bachelor's degree in political science from Carleton University and is a Fellow of the National Academy of Human Resources.
Douglas R. Bettinger, age 59, is the Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer of Lam Research Corporation, a semiconductor equipment company, with responsibility for Finance, Tax, Treasury, Investor Relations and Corporate Analytics, and has served at Lam Research since 2013. Prior to joining Lam Research, Mr. Bettinger served as Senior Vice President and Chief Financial Officer of Avago Technologies (now Broadcom Inc.) from 2008 to 2013. From 2007 to 2008, he served as Vice President of Finance and Corporate Controller at Xilinx, Inc., and from 2004 to 2007, he was Chief Financial Officer at 24/7 Customer. Mr. Bettinger worked at Intel Corporation from 1993 to 2004, where he held several senior-level finance positions. Mr. Bettinger currently serves on the board of directors of Lattice Semiconductor Corporation and the Industrial Advisory Board of the University of Wisconsin College of Engineering, and from 2018 to 2025 served on the SEMI Board of Industry Leaders. Mr. Bettinger earned an M.B.A. in finance from the University of Michigan and a B.S. in economics from the University of Wisconsin–Madison.
Sasan K. Goodarzi, age 58, has served as President and Chief Executive Officer and a member of the board of directors of Intuit Inc., a global financial technology platform company, since January 2019, and as Chairman of its board of directors since January 2026. He previously served as Executive Vice President and General Manager of Intuit's Small Business Group from 2016 to 2018, Executive Vice President and General Manager of Intuit's Consumer Tax Group from 2015 to 2016, Senior Vice President and General Manager of the Consumer Tax Group from 2013 to 2015, and Senior Vice President and Chief Information Officer from 2011 to 2013, having rejoined Intuit after serving as Chief Executive Officer of Nexant Inc. beginning in November 2010. During his previous tenure at Intuit from 2004 to 2010, Mr. Goodarzi led several business units. Prior to Intuit, he served as Global President of the Products group at Invensys and held senior leadership roles at Honeywell Inc. From April 2018 to January 2026, Mr. Goodarzi served on the board of directors of Atlassian Corporation. He holds a bachelor's degree in electrical engineering from the University of Central Florida and an M.B.A. from the Kellogg School of Management at Northwestern University.
There are no family relationships between any of Ms. Morris, Mr. Bettinger or Mr. Goodarzi and any other director or executive officer of the Company. There are no transactions between any of Ms. Morris, Mr. Bettinger or Mr. Goodarzi, or any member of their immediate families, and the Company that would be reportable under Item 404(a) of Regulation S-K. Further, there is no arrangement or understanding between any of Ms. Morris, Mr. Bettinger or Mr. Goodarzi and any other persons or entities pursuant to which he or she was appointed as a director of the Company.
Each of Ms. Morris, Mr. Bettinger and Mr. Goodarzi will participate in all director compensation and benefit programs in which the Company's other non-employee directors participate, including an annual director retainer of $100,000 and an annual equity grant of restricted stock units valued at $250,000. In addition, each of Ms. Morris and Mr. Goodarzi will receive an annual Executive Compensation Committee member fee of $10,000 and Mr. Bettinger will receive an annual Audit Committee member fee of $15,000. Upon joining the Board, each of them received a restricted stock unit award valued in an amount equal to a prorated portion of the annual equity grant, which prorated grant will vest on the date of the 2027 annual meeting of stockholders. The Company also expects to enter into its standard form of indemnification agreement with each of Ms. Morris, Mr. Bettinger and Mr. Goodarzi, the form of which was filed as Exhibit 10.1 to the Company's Form 8-K filed on April 20, 2021 and is incorporated herein by reference.

SANTA CLARA, Calif., November 12, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- NVIDIA (NASDAQ: NVDA) Board of Directors announced today that Jensen Huang has resigned as President, Chief Executive Officer, and a member of the Board, effective immediately.
Colette Kress, current Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer of NVIDIA, has agreed to serve as Interim Chief Executive Officer. Kress will continue to serve as Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer while serving as Interim Chief Executive Officer until a permanent successor has been named. CONSUMER PRICE INDEX - OCTOBER 2026
The Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U) increased 0.4 percent on a seasonally adjusted basis in October 
after rising 0.6 percent in September, the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics reported today. 
The index for shelter rose 0.3 percent in October, accounting for over thirty percent of the monthly all items increase. 
The food index increased 0.5 percent in October, as the food at home index rose 0.4 percent and the food away from home 
index increased 0.5 percent. The index for energy increased 0.7 percent over the month following a 5.2-percent increase 
in September. 
The index for all items less food and energy rose 0.3 percent in October, as it did in September and August. Indexes that 
increased over the month include recreation, medical care, motor vehicle insurance, household furnishings and operations, 
and education. Conversely, the index for used cars and trucks and the index for communication were among the small number 
of major indexes that decreased in October.

Food
The index for food rose 0.5 percent in October after being unchanged in September. The food at home index increased 0.4 
percent over the month. Four of the six major grocery store food group indexes increased in October, while one index 
decreased. The index for other food at home increased 0.7 percent in October, as the index for snacks rose 1.0 percent. 
The meats, poultry, fish, and eggs index increased 0.5 percent over the month, as the beef index rose 0.9 percent. The 
index for fruits and vegetables and the index for dairy and related products each increased 0.6 percent in October. 
In contrast, the nonalcoholic beverages index decreased 0.3 percent in October, after rising 0.9 percent in September. 
The index for cereals and bakery products was unchanged over the month.
The food away from home index rose 0.5 percent in October. The index for full service meals rose 0.7 percent, and the 
index for limited service meals increased 0.4 percent over the month.
Energy
The index for energy increased 0.7 percent in October after rising 5.2 percent in September. The gasoline index increased 
1.0 percent over the month, after advancing 9.1 percent the previous month. (Before seasonal adjustment, gasoline prices 
decreased 0.7 percent in October.) The index for electricity rose 0.9 percent over the month. In contrast, the natural 
gas index decreased 0.8 percent in October.
All items less food and energy
The index for all items less food and energy rose 0.3 percent in October, as it did in September and August. The shelter 
index increased 0.3 percent over the month after rising 0.4 percent in September. The index for owners' equivalent rent 
rose 0.3 percent in October, and the index for rent increased 0.2 percent. The lodging away from home index rose 0.6 
percent in October after rising 2.0 percent the previous month.
The index for recreation increased 0.8 percent over the month after rising 0.5 percent in September. The motor vehicle 
insurance index rose 0.7 percent in October, and the household furnishings and operations index increased 0.2 percent. 
The index for education increased 0.3 percent in October, and the index for new vehicles rose 0.2 percent. The personal 
care index, the airline fares index, and the apparel index also increased over the month.
The medical care index increased 0.3 percent in October after rising 0.1 percent in September. The index for hospital 
services rose 0.8 percent over the month, and the index for physicians' services increased 0.4 percent. The prescription 
drugs index rose 0.3 percent in October. 
The index for used cars and trucks declined 1.2 percent in October after rising 0.7 percent in September. The 
communication index decreased 0.1 percent over the month.
Not seasonally adjusted CPI measures
The Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U) increased to an index level of 337.511 (1982-84=100). For the 
month, the index rose 0.2 percent prior to seasonal adjustment. 
The Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W) increased to an index level of 331.147 
(1982-84=100). For the month, the index increased 0.1 percent prior to seasonal adjustment. 
For the month, the Chained Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (C-CPI-U) increased 0.2 percent on a not 
seasonally adjusted basis. Please note that the indexes for the past 10 to 12 months are subject to revision. 
_______________
The Consumer Price Index news release for November 2026 is scheduled to be published on Thursday, December 10, 2026, 
at 8:30 a.m. (ET).
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
 Upcoming Consumer Price Index Publication Changes
With the publication of January 2027 CPI data on February 11, 2027, several index titles will change: 
"wireless telephone services" will change to "wireless telephone service"; "physicians' services" will change 
to "physician services"; and "music instruments and accessories" will change to "music instruments and 
accessories including instrument rentals." More information is available online at 
www.bls.gov/cpi/additional-resources/series-title-changes.htm
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Technical Note
Brief Explanation of the CPI
The Consumer Price Index (CPI) measures the change in prices paid by consumers for goods and services. The CPI reflects
spending patterns for each of two population groups: all urban consumers and urban wage earners and clerical workers.
The all urban consumer group represents over 90 percent of the total U.S. population. It is based on the expenditures
of almost all residents of urban or metropolitan areas, including professionals, the self-employed, the poor, the
unemployed, and retired people, as well as urban wage earners and clerical workers. Not included in the CPI are the
spending patterns of people living in rural nonmetropolitan areas, farming families, people in the Armed Forces, and
those in institutions, such as prisons and mental hospitals. Consumer inflation for all urban consumers is measured by
two indexes, namely, the Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U) and the Chained Consumer Price Index for
All Urban Consumers (C-CPI-U). 
The Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W) is based on the expenditures of households
included in the CPI-U definition that meet two requirements: more than one-half of the household's income must come
from clerical or wage occupations, and at least one of the household's earners must have been employed for at least 37
weeks during the previous 12 months. The CPI-W population represents approximately 30 percent of the total U.S.
population and is a subset of the CPI-U population.
The CPIs are based on prices of food, clothing, shelter, fuels, transportation, doctors' and dentists' services, drugs,
and other goods and services that people buy for day-to-day living. Prices are collected each month in 75 urban areas
across the country from about 6,000 housing units and approximately 22,000 retail establishments (department stores,
supermarkets, hospitals, and other types of stores and service establishments). All taxes directly associated with the
purchase and use of items are included in the index. Prices of fuels and a few other items are obtained every month in
all 75 locations. Prices of most other commodities and services are collected every month in the three largest
geographic areas and every other month in other areas. Prices of most goods and services are obtained by personal
visit, telephone call, web, or app collection by the Bureau's trained representatives.
In calculating the index, price changes for the various items in each location are aggregated using weights, which
represent their importance in the spending of the appropriate population group. Local data are then combined to obtain
a U.S. city average. For the CPI-U and CPI-W, separate indexes are also published by size of city, by region of the
country, for cross-classifications of regions and population-size classes, and for 23 selected local areas. Area
indexes do not measure differences in the level of prices among cities; they only measure the average change in prices
for each area since the base period. For the C-CPI-U, data are issued only at the national level. The CPI-U and CPI-W
are considered final when released, but the C-CPI-U is issued in preliminary form and subject to three subsequent
quarterly revisions.

 THE EMPLOYMENT SITUATION - OCTOBER 2026 
Total nonfarm payroll employment rose by 165,000 in October, and the unemployment rate changed 
little at 4.1 percent, the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics reported today. Employment increased in 
professional and business services, in health care, and in transportation and warehousing. 
This news release presents statistics from two monthly surveys. The household survey measures labor 
force status, including unemployment, by demographic characteristics. The establishment survey 
measures nonfarm employment, hours, and earnings by industry. For more information about the 
concepts and statistical methodology used in these two surveys, see the Technical Note. 
Household Survey Data 
Both the unemployment rate, at 4.1 percent, and the number of unemployed people, at 7.1 million, 
changed little in October. The unemployment rate has remained in a narrow range of 4.1 percent to 
4.3 percent since March. (See table A-1.) 
Among the major worker groups, the unemployment rates showed little or no change in October for 
adult men (3.9 percent), adult women (3.6 percent), teenagers (13.9 percent), and people who are 
White (3.7 percent), Black (6.6 percent), Asian (2.8 percent), or Hispanic (4.7 percent). (See 
tables A-1, A-2, and A-3.) 
The number of long-term unemployed (those jobless for 27 weeks or more), at 2.0 million, changed 
little over the month. The long-term unemployed accounted for 27.6 percent of all unemployed 
people. (See table A-12.) 
Both the labor force participation rate, at 61.9 percent, and the employment-population ratio, at 
59.3 percent, changed little in October. These measures have shown little net change since January. 
(See table A-1.) 
The number of people employed part time for economic reasons increased by 339,000 to 4.8 million in 
October. These individuals would have preferred full-time employment but were working part time 
because their hours had been reduced or they were unable to find full-time jobs. (See table A-8.) 
In October, the number of people not in the labor force who currently want a job changed little at 
6.0 million. These individuals were not counted as unemployed because they were not actively 
looking for work during the 4 weeks preceding the survey or were unavailable to take a job. (See 
table A-1.) 
Among those not in the labor force who wanted a job, the number of people marginally attached to 
the labor force changed little at 1.6 million in October. These individuals wanted and were 
available for work and had looked for a job sometime in the prior 12 months but had not looked for 
work in the 4 weeks preceding the survey. The number of discouraged workers, a subset of the 
marginally attached who believed that no jobs were available for them, also changed little over 
the month at 448,000. (See Summary table A.) 
Establishment Survey Data 
Total nonfarm payroll employment rose by 165,000 in October, higher than the average monthly gain 
of 48,000 over the prior 12 months. In October, employment increased in professional and business 
services, in health care, and in transportation and warehousing. (See table B-1.) 
Employment in professional and business services increased by 70,000 in October, well above the 
average monthly gain of 15,000 over the prior 12 months. In October, employment continued to trend 
up in professional, scientific, and technical services (+33,000), in administrative and support and 
waste management and remediation services (+28,000), and in management of companies and enterprises 
(+9,000). Professional and business services has added 269,000 jobs since a recent low in October 
2025. 
Health care added 42,000 jobs in October, higher than the average monthly gain of 31,000 over the 
prior 12 months. In October, employment gains occurred in hospitals (+16,000), home health care 
services (+11,000), and outpatient care centers (+5,000). 
In October, transportation and warehousing added 25,000 jobs, reflecting growth in couriers and 
messengers (+17,000) and air transportation (+4,000). Transportation and warehousing has added 
104,000 jobs since a recent employment low in February, with couriers and messengers (+71,000) 
contributing most of the gain. 
Manufacturing employment continued to trend up in October (+19,000) and has increased by 101,000 
since a recent low in December 2025. In October, job gains occurred in computer and electronic 
product manufacturing (+7,000), machinery manufacturing (+4,000), and primary metal manufacturing 
(+4,000). 
Employment showed little change over the month in other major industries, including mining, 
quarrying, and oil and gas extraction; construction; wholesale trade; retail trade; information; 
financial activities; social assistance; leisure and hospitality; other services; and government. 
In October, average hourly earnings for all employees on private nonfarm payrolls increased by 14 
cents, or 0.4 percent, to $38.00. Over the past 12 months, average hourly earnings have increased 
by 3.1 percent. In October, average hourly earnings of private-sector production and nonsupervisory 
employees rose by 12 cents, or 0.4 percent, to $32.75. (See tables B-3 and B-8.) 
The average workweek for all employees on private nonfarm payrolls remained at 34.4 hours in 
October. In manufacturing, the average workweek was unchanged at 40.5 hours, and overtime edged up 
by 0.1 hour to 3.1 hours. The average workweek for production and nonsupervisory employees on 
private nonfarm payrolls declined by 0.1 hour to 33.8 hours. (See tables B-2 and B-7.) 
The change in total nonfarm payroll employment for August was revised up by 53,000, from +133,000 
to +186,000, and the change for September was revised up by 31,000, from +29,000 to +60,000. With 
these revisions, employment in August and September combined is 84,000 higher than previously 
reported. (Monthly revisions result from additional reports received from businesses and government 
agencies since the last published estimates and from the recalculation of seasonal factors.) 
_____________ 
The Employment Situation for November 2026 is scheduled to be published on Friday, December 4, 
2026, at 8:30 a.m. (ET).

 PRODUCER PRICE INDEXES - OCTOBER 2026
The Producer Price Index for final demand rose 0.3 percent in October, seasonally adjusted, the 
U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics reported today. Final demand prices advanced 1.4 percent in 
September and 0.4 percent in August. (See table A.) On an unadjusted basis, the index for final 
demand increased 6.5 percent for the 12 months ended in October, the largest 12-month rise 
since moving up 7.4 percent in November 2022.
Leading the October advance in final demand prices, the index for final demand goods increased 
0.5 percent. Prices for final demand services moved up 0.2 percent.
The index for final demand less foods, energy, and trade services rose 0.5 percent in October, the 
same as in September. For the 12 months ended in October, prices for final demand less foods, 
energy, and trade services advanced 4.9 percent.
Final Demand
Final demand goods: The index for final demand goods increased 0.5 percent in October following 
a 2.5-percent rise in September. Over 60 percent of the advance in October is attributable to prices 
for final demand goods less foods and energy, which moved up 0.5 percent. The index for final 
demand foods increased 1.3 percent. In contrast, prices for final demand energy edged down 0.1 
percent. For the 12 months ended in October, the index for final demand goods increased 10.2 
percent, the largest 12-month rise since advancing 10.5 percent in October 2022.
Product detail: Within the index for final demand goods in October, prices for basic organic 
chemicals advanced 3.9 percent. The indexes for fresh and dry vegetables; gas fuels; aeronautical, 
nautical, and navigational instruments; jet fuel; and processed young chickens also moved higher. 
(See table 2.) Conversely, diesel fuel prices fell 7.9 percent. The indexes for pork and for passenger 
cars also declined. 
Final demand services: The index for final demand services moved up 0.2 percent in October, the 
fifth consecutive advance. Three-fourths of the October rise can be traced to a 2.0-percent increase in 
prices for final demand transportation and warehousing services. The index for final demand services 
less trade, transportation, and warehousing advanced 0.2 percent. In contrast, margins for final 
demand trade services decreased 0.2 percent.
Product detail: Over 80 percent of the October increase in the index for final demand services is 
attributable to prices for truck transportation of freight, which rose 3.9 percent. The indexes for fuels 
and lubricants retailing; health, beauty, and optical goods retailing; food and alcohol wholesaling; 
hospital outpatient care; and traveler accommodation services also moved higher. Conversely, 
margins for machinery and vehicle wholesaling fell 4.2 percent. Prices for system software 
publishing and for airline passenger services also declined.

EIA forecasts Alaskan crude oil production to grow 13% in 2027 
 Data source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, Short-Term Energy Outlook, November 2026 
After decades of decline, crude oil production in Alaska is growing, driven by two projects on Alaska’s North Slope. In our latest Short-Term Energy Outlook, we expect a 23,000 barrels per day (b/d) (6%) increase in 2026, followed by a 60,000 b/d (13%) rise in 2027. At a forecast 505,000 b/d in 2027, output would be the most since 2014. 
If realized, these annual production increases will be the largest since the 1980s, when Alaskan crude production peaked at 2.0 million b/d. 
The recent growth is attributable to two projects on Alaska's North Slope: 
The Nuna project, owned by ConocoPhillips, started production in December 2024 and is expected to produce 20,000 b/d at its peak. So far this year, it has produced an average of 10,000 b/d, partially offsetting existing production declines. 
The Pikka Phase 1 project, jointly owned by Santos and Repsol, began production in May 2026 with initial average monthly production of 2,000 b/d and reaching 38,000 b/d as of September 2026, according to data from the Alaska Oil & Gas Conservation Commission. We expect peak production of 80,000 b/d by winter 2026–27, nearly 20% of total Alaskan production in 2025. 
Notably, our STEO production data indicate that third-quarter 2026 production grew 4% as Pikka Phase 1 came online, marking the first third-quarter production increase in more than 40 years. Alaskan crude output typically dips in late summer when operators conduct annual maintenance, running an average of 7% lower than first-quarter levels over the previous five years (2021–2025).
